doc.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005

title: Forest Club, the Frolicks and the New Orleans club scene
summary: Howard Voorhees gets him the Forest Club and Orpheum jobs; late-night clubs, white bands, and Earl Hines on Rampart Street.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Right. Well at that time it was eighth grade and then started first year. Yeah. But Howard Vorhees got me the job at the Forest Club. It was a gambling house. They didn’t call them casinos then. And we would play for dancing and so forth while people gambled. And then he finally got me to go into the Orpheum Theater. He came the contractor. He says, “Kid, I’m going to get you here.” And I started at the Orpheum Theater. Then after a while he got the job at The Frolicks night club, only a couple of blocks, where Louis Prima was. He was playing in another place. Oh the clubs were all over, live music you know, five, six, ten piece bands. And after the Orpheum at eleven o’clock, we’d go and play until five in the morning. And I’d be playing you know.
At that time, in New Orleans, King Oliver and Louis Armstrong, those guys had already gone north.
But was there still a sense that this was the hotbed of jazz?

Oh yes, absolutely. But you know all the clubs — I can’t think of all the band leaders and trumpet players — Al Marico was one of the great trumpet players there. They were all white, all white in the clubs.
So there was nobody who kind of took that—

But there was black section there. Earl Hines came in. I will never forget, on Rampart Street, one of the clubs there. Earl “Fatha” Hines. He came. But most of the clubs, LaVita was a famous club, the Roosevelt Hotel, and oh there was jazz all over.
But was it pretty, was it sort of segregated communities too?
